The last five reactions were +0.7, -5.5, +1.1, +17.0 and -15.3%, median abs 5.5% (baseline, from 8-K acceptance times). Huge run-up into the print: the close went from 15.18 on 11-05 (near the 52w low) to 20.76 on 11-06 (+36.8%, the AST SpaceMobile engine and licence deal, >$1.3B over 3 years) and 24.31 on 11-09 (+17.1%, NASA CLPS 2 vendor selection, announced 11-07), then 23.29 today on the Synspective deal for up to 10 Alpha launches (Yahoo daily bars; Firefly newsroom). The 5-day run-up is +37%, but the stock is still 60% off its high and 39% below where it stood before the last print. Consensus: Q3 revenue $103.8-106.3M (EW 11-03; Benzinga snapshot about late September), EPS -$0.49 to -$0.52. Q4 consensus about $137M (Benzinga, stale). The FY26 guide is $420-450M, reaffirmed 08-11 with launches cut from four to three, '95% booked at midpoint'. H1 revenue was about $199M, so consensus implies a record Q4 near $135M. Short interest is roughly 6-11% of float (sources conflict; 10.8M shares 09-21). A resale-registration POS AM was filed 11-02, an overhang.
view: This print turns on three things the deal week has pulled together: (1) the 2026 guide and Q4, (2) the Alpha Block II Flight 8 date, and (3) how the AST licence and engineering money is booked and when the cash arrives. On (2) the public trace leans negative. On 08-11 management said acceptance testing would start 'in the next few weeks', then delivery to Vandenberg, static fire, integration and launch, with two Alpha launches in Q4. Since then Firefly has issued nine press releases (cleanroom, SSC, Starcloud, SciTec twice, MoonFall PDR, AST, CLPS 2, Synspective) and none of them reports that acceptance testing is complete, that the vehicle has shipped or that a static fire has happened. Launch Library still lists every Alpha Block 2 mission as NET 2026-12-31, TBD. So two Q4 launches look very unlikely, and even one is doubtful. The Q4 consensus near $137M is stale against that. The offset is that launch revenue is small (Q2: launch $9.4M against spacecraft $108.3M), spacecraft revenue is recognised over time, and the midpoint was '95% booked'. A slip therefore threatens the guide by tens of millions, which probably means a narrowing toward the $420M low end rather than a collapse. The stock has already lost more than half its value since spring on Alpha execution, so a further slip is the expected disappointment rather than a shock. Against that, (3) can surprise either way and is much larger. If any of the roughly $800M licence (half cash, half AST stock) or the engineering services is recognised in Q4, or if management gives a 2027 framework with the deal in it, the headline guide could rise sharply. Equally, a deal that books slowly, carries large costs and pays in restricted AST stock would let the run-up deflate. The deal week has already added about $1.4B of market value, roughly the headline value of a deal that is mostly margin on the licence, so the price holds the deal at about face value. I cannot show that the price is wrong on either side. A crowded week-long rally before a print that is likely to carry a launch slip tilts me slightly down, but not far enough to bet.
unpriced: Partly: the Q4 consensus (~$137M) and the FY guide assume two Q4 Alpha launches, and since August there is no public sign that Flight 8 has finished acceptance testing or reached Vandenberg. That gap is real, but it is small next to the deal's unknown accounting, and the stock has already de-rated on Alpha execution. Not strong enough to call a direction.

recommendation.reason: The one dated, checkable gap is that Flight 8 has no public trace of acceptance testing, shipment or static fire, against a stale Q4 consensus that needs launches. But launch revenue is a small slice of a largely booked year, and the AST deal's revenue recognition and cash timing could swamp it in either direction on the call. With a 37% five-day run-up on deal news, a slight downside lean is all the evidence supports.
recommendation.what_would_flip_it: Management recognising part of the AST licence or engineering services in Q4, or raising the FY26 guide or giving a 2027 outlook that includes the deal, would make this an upside print despite any Flight 8 slip.

self_critique: The strongest case against my lean is the company's own history. In Nov 2025 it raised guidance while Alpha was grounded and the stock gapped up 17%. Spacecraft and SciTec revenue have repeatedly beaten (Q2 by 34%), and a Q3 consensus below Q2's actual is an easy bar. On top of that, management gets a whole call to frame the AST cash, the CLPS 2 selection and the Synspective manifest. A quarter's absence of Flight 8 press releases is weak evidence, and the company may simply hold news until the call. My downside lean rests mostly on the run-up, and I cannot show that it is mispriced.
approach_notes: The 'freshest data first' rule and reading the company's own press-release stream for what it does NOT say (Flight 8 silence) paid. Asking 'who would know' reached the Launch Library API, which was a useful physical trace. 'Priced in is a claim to prove' was hard to apply here because the dominant new fact, the AST deal, has undisclosed accounting, so the analysis could not get past its uncertainty.
